findings.where: Motion sketch panel, the easing note under the curve ('Easing cubic-bezier(0.5, 0, 0.2, 1): a stone lowered onto its bed…'), at both widths
findings.fault: The curve value is set in the browser's default monospace. That is a third typeface outside the stated Cinzel and Alegreya Sans pair, and it sits visibly larger and heavier than the small sans around it. In a tile whose job is to fix the type pair, it reads as a code fragment left in the client's copy.
findings.who_objects: Mark, reading the tile as his site's look, sees a typewriter-like face the type note never mentions. The round-2 designer also can't tell whether a mono face belongs to the identity. The house DNA bans the default font stack as a voice.

findings.where: Article page specimen: the byline 'MMM INFRA BLOG NO. 8 · 18 SEPTEMBER 2024' under the title, compared with the lecture line 'Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF' at the foot of the same article. Worst on phone, where the tracked byline breaks and leaves '2024' alone on a second line.
findings.fault: Two parts of the same article that do the same job (the date and kind of an item) get two different treatments. The blog byline is in tracked Cinzel capitals, and the lecture line is in plain Alegreya Sans. Setting the byline in Cinzel also breaks the tile's own type note, which keeps Cinzel for section headings, the nav and the button only. The wide tracking is what forces the phone byline to wrap onto an orphaned year.
findings.who_objects: Angélique, adding a post or a PDF, has no clear rule for how a date line is set. The round-2 designer gets a specimen that contradicts its own note. A reader on a phone sees a ragged byline.

findings.where: Motion sketch panel, the easing curve drawn in minium red, at both widths
findings.fault: The curve is drawn in minium. The palette caption says minium is 'the one action only', and the texture note says the same. So the tile itself uses the action red on a static diagram, right above the outlined 'Lay again' button, which is not red.
findings.who_objects: The animation and layout rounds take this tile as their colour rule. Here it shows red used decoratively, which undoes the 'one accent flows to the action' idea the direction is built on. A visitor also sees red on something that does nothing.

findings.where: Article page specimen, the pull quote's double-ruled frame, at both widths
findings.fault: The quote's heavy double rule (a thick outer line and a thin inner one) is the strongest edge on the page. Every other framed part has a single hairline: the portrait stand-in, the texture tile, the motion panel and the 'Lay again' button. So a static aside in running text is framed more heavily than any panel or control. In the article it outweighs the headline and the body.
findings.who_objects: A reader of an article page gets pulled to a side remark before the argument. The round-2 designer can't tell which border weight the identity uses, so edges are not treated alike.
